memory_leads.lead: Shipboard operational technology spans a control chain rather than one automation box: engineering crew and technical management operate and maintain machinery while sensors, controllers, actuators, alarm/monitoring systems and maker/service support jointly determine whether commanded physical behavior is trustworthy.

Machinery-control mode is a state variable. Local/manual, remote, automatic and fallback modes can have different available functions, response times and staffing needs; a system may remain physically operable after automation is degraded.

Automation separates commanded state, measured state and actual physical state. A bad sensor, actuator or control loop can make displayed or commanded values diverge from what machinery is really doing, so control-system agreement is not automatically physical truth.

Alarm state is an operational information layer: alarms may be active, acknowledged, inhibited/suppressed, standing or cleared, and the history of those transitions can matter when reconstructing how crews understood a developing fault.

Alarm floods and cascades can turn many individually valid signals into a workload and prioritization problem. The structural risk is not simply too many alarms but loss of causal ordering and attention during a disturbance.

Condition monitoring creates a separate judgment chain from failure itself: vibration, temperature, pressure, oil/debris or other trends may trigger inspection or maintenance decisions before equipment crosses a hard failure threshold.

Predictive or condition-based maintenance should preserve the distinction between measured anomaly, diagnostic interpretation, maintenance recommendation and later observed component condition; an alert is not itself proof of a defect.

Software and configuration are part of vessel operational state. Parameter sets, control logic, firmware/software versions, calibration and configuration changes can alter machinery behavior without a visible change to the mechanical equipment.

Remote diagnostics/support introduces a shore dependency: crew may remain the physical operator while shore technical teams or equipment specialists inspect data, advise settings or support fault isolation through communications links.

Remote-access readiness has two sides—availability and trust. Loss of connectivity can delay diagnosis, while uncontrolled or compromised access can itself become an operational risk; the exact cyber mechanism is deferred.

OT cyber compromise is structurally different from ordinary IT inconvenience when it can affect control, sensing, alarms or availability of propulsion, auxiliaries or cargo systems. Blind recall should retain the propagation topology, not assert any specific incident.

Redundancy only protects availability when failure domains are sufficiently independent. Duplicate pumps, controllers or displays can still share power, communications, software/configuration or sensors, creating common-mode loss analogous to P026 bridge-information coupling.

Degraded OT can reduce effective capacity without immobilizing a vessel: manual operation, conservative machinery limits, extra watchkeeping, reduced propulsion or unavailable cargo auxiliaries can preserve safety while increasing voyage time or port stay.

The atlas technology/operations axis should represent digitalization as changed failure and recovery topology—sensing, control, configuration, communications and remote support—not simply as adoption of newer equipment.

P011-style maintenance/availability logic is refined because condition-monitoring alerts and remote diagnostics are intermediate Judgment states between equipment condition and a maintenance action; later teardown or failure Outcome must not rewrite the earlier diagnosis.

P026 information-integrity logic generalizes below the bridge: multiple machinery displays or alarms may share one sensor or controller, so apparently corroborating digital indications can have a common source.

Operational availability should distinguish loss of automation from loss of physical plant. A truthful replay can show a vessel operating under manual or restricted mode rather than collapsing every control-system fault into complete off-hire.
Generic onboard alarms, sensor degradation and degraded-mode fallback were introduced in P026 for navigation; P027 retains only their machinery/control-system-specific propagation.

General machinery failure, maintenance and off-hire effects belong to earlier vessel-technical coverage; P027 adds the OT/control/monitoring information layer rather than another mechanical component inventory.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.reason: Blind memory supports functional roles and failure domains but cannot establish product capabilities, software versions or installation lineages.
Incident identity, technical compromise path and attribution require source-grounded cyber or casualty Evidence.
Requirements and implementation dates vary by regime and vessel and require claim-scoped regulatory Evidence.
Exact thresholds/configuration and current operating condition require vessel-specific records and source-first Evidence.

stop_reason: The shipboard OT chain is populated from actor/control-mode and measured-versus-physical state through alarms, condition-monitoring judgment, software/configuration, remote support/cyber dependence, redundancy and degraded operation. Further recall becomes vendor-, software-version-, rule-, cyber-incident-, casualty- or vessel-specific.
truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation; no vendor capability, software/configuration version, regulatory requirement, condition-monitoring accuracy, cyber incident, casualty cause or vessel-specific OT condition is verified.
